name: object-mother
intent: Centralise the creation of ready-made, valid domain objects in one factory so that every test across the suite starts from the same named, well-understood fixtures instead of rebuilding object graphs by hand.
problem: Tests throughout a codebase need valid instances of the same domain objects, and constructing them by hand - wiring value objects, dependent entities, identities and required collections - is verbose and duplicated in every test class. The copies drift apart, churn whenever a constructor or validation rule changes, and let a test fail for accidental setup reasons rather than the behaviour under test; a per-class setUp/BeforeEach method cannot be shared between test classes.
context: Applies to test suites over a domain model with real invariants: entities and aggregates with many required fields, value objects, dependent objects and identity rules, where a handful of named business scenarios (an employee hired last week, an overdue invoice, a VIP customer) can be reused across many test classes. The mother belongs to test sources and is meaningless in production code; where every test needs unique data rather than a shared canonical example, a Test Data Builder fits better.
benefits: One place defines what a valid instance looks like, so tests read as the behaviour under test instead of as object construction.
Named canned objects ('a customer who just signed up') become a shared vocabulary across the team, tests and even discussions with domain experts.
Reuse beyond a single test class: unlike a per-class setUp fixture, the mother serves every suite and can be moved into a shared test-support package.
Single point of change: a new required field or constructor parameter is fixed once, in the mother, instead of in every test that builds that object.
Consistency of test data: every test starts from objects that satisfy the domain's invariants, reducing false failures caused by malformed setup.
tradeoffs: Heavy coupling to exact canned data: many tests depend on the values the mother returns, so changing a standard fixture ripples through the whole suite (Fowler's stated fault of the pattern).

Poor fit for variation: every slightly different need invites another factory method, and the mother either bloats with fine-grained duplicated construction code or explodes into methods containing a single new statement (Pryce's criticism).
Canned defaults can overfit assertions: a test that only passes because the mother supplies a particular value proves less than it appears to.
Misleading validity: a mother (or a generator beneath it) that fills fields without the domain's own validation can produce objects that cannot exist in production and hide real bugs.
Shared-mutable-fixture risk: handing out a cached instance or a graph with shared nested objects lets one test's mutation change another test's starting state.
Indirection cost: a mother with one or two consumers adds a layer and a name to learn without buying reuse.

participants.responsibility: Factory (class, module or object) that owns the construction knowledge and returns ready-made, valid instances, one creation method per named fixture or business scenario.
Requests a named fixture instead of constructing the graph, and tweaks the result only for the detail the test asserts on.
The entities and value objects being instantiated; they stay unaware of the mother and keep enforcing their own invariants through normal constructors.
The named sample instance (e.g. the newly hired employee) whose data is stable enough for many tests to reference and reason about.

use_cases: Domain aggregates with many required fields and cross-field invariants are needed in dozens of test classes (an employee with marital status, dependents and payroll history).
Persistence or ORM tests need valid saved entities with stable identities and the related rows the schema requires.
The suite must exercise named business scenarios (VIP customer, trial account, overdue invoice) that should mean the same thing everywhere.
A regression suite wants the same fixture data as before a refactor, so behaviour changes show up instead of being masked by rewritten setup.
Contract or integration tests across services need the same canonical examples in several codebases, behind one mother per language.
Microsoft's EF4/EF6 testability guidance uses EmployeeObjectMother.CreateEmployees() to supply shared employees across MVC controller test fixtures.
The Python object-mother-pattern package provides reusable mother classes for valid and invalid values plus composed collections, giving Python suites a concrete implementation of the pattern.
Java's Matriarch library exposes a Mother factory with JUnit integration and field overrides; it is an Object Mother-style option when canonical fixtures need controlled variation.
avoid_when: Each test mostly needs its own unique data: a Test Data Builder with valid defaults lets the test state only what it asserts.
Only one test class needs the objects: a private helper or the class's own setUp/BeforeEach method is simpler and keeps the data local.
The object is a trivial value with one or two fields: constructing it inline states the value more clearly than a named fixture hides it.
The data must be randomized or anonymized per run (property-based tests, load data): use a generator/faker instead of canned examples.
The domain type already supplies a meaningful default (constructor defaults, data-class defaults, Default trait) that the fixture would only duplicate.
anti_patterns: The god mother: one global TestData/AllMothers class with dozens of createXWithY methods, accumulating duplicated construction code until nobody dares change it.
Canned-data overfit: tests assert values they only know because the mother returns them, so changing the fixture silently rewrites the expected results and the assertion stops checking anything.
Shared mutable fixture: the mother caches an instance or hands out nested collections by reference, so a mutating test corrupts every later test (order-dependent failures).
Mother as database seeder: commit/rollback, clock control and cleanup hidden inside the factory, turning unit tests into order-dependent integration tests.
Production dependency: domain or service code importing the test mother because it was a convenient place to get a 'default' object.
design_principles: Single point of change for valid construction: new required state is added once, in the mother.
Separation of concerns: fixture data (which objects) stays apart from test logic (what behaviour is asserted).
Don't repeat yourself across test classes - reuse through a shared test-support unit rather than copy-paste setup.
Encapsulation: the mother owns the knowledge of which fields must be set together for the object to be valid.
Ubiquitous language: fixture names reflect domain scenarios, so tests speak the same vocabulary as the business.
best_practices: Keep one mother per domain class or aggregate (CustomerMother, InvoiceMother) instead of a single catch-all test-data class.
Always return a freshly constructed graph; never cache instances or share nested mutable objects between calls.
Name creation methods after business meaning ('aCustomerWhoJustSignedUp'), not after implementation details ('createCustomerWithTwoOrders').
Route creation through the domain's real constructors and validation so the fixtures cannot represent impossible states.
Add variation sparingly; when a second or third tweak appears, compose a Test Data Builder underneath the mother for the canonical examples.
Keep the mother in test sources (or a test-support package) and give it no production dependencies; seed fakers and sequences so runs stay deterministic.
sources: Meszaros, G., xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code, Addison-Wesley (2007) - Object Mother, the test-fixture strategy pattern for shared ready-made objects (catalog provenance).
